job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: Archaeologists have recently uncovered new details about the daily life of the Harappan people. Unlike later civilizations that left behind written records, the Harappans remain a mystery because their unique script has never been deciphered. Excavations show that these people were master builders who used baked bricks, which were far more durable than simple dried mud, to construct their multi-roomed houses. In the heart of their cities, they built a large, watertight tank known as the Great Bath. This structure was likely used for special religious rituals rather than for recreation or swimming. The Harappans were also skilled traders who used square stone seals to mark their goods, acting like a stamp for identification rather than as currency for buying items. While the civilization eventually faded, the people did not simply vanish or die out in a single war. Instead, they likely migrated to other regions as climate changes and shifting rivers made their original cities difficult to sustain. Their legacy lived on through the knowledge passed down to future generations, proving that the Harappan culture transformed rather than completely disappeared.

items.evidence: Excavations show that these people were master builders who used baked bricks, which were far more durable than simple dried mud, to construct their multi-roomed houses.
items.q: Why were Harappan houses strong enough to last for so long?
options: They were built with hard-baked bricks
They were built with thick mud walls
They were built with iron-tipped tools
They were built with many small rooms
items.explain: Baked bricks were far more durable than dried mud, so the multi-roomed houses were strong.
